about: Pictures shown on cards. Each one is a file on Wikimedia Commons, linked, not copied. Author, credit and licence are read from the Commons API by tools/commons-credits.mjs. See js/images.mjs for the rules.

images.shows: Pages 60–61 of Georg Waitz's 1883 printed edition of the Annals of St-Bertin, the edition cited on this card. The entry for 862 is on page 60: “qui Ungri vocantur” (“who are called Ungri”) is near the top, in the blue highlight.
images.shows_basis: Claude read the page heading (“Annales Bertiniani auctore Hincmaro. 862.”) and the words “qui Ungri vocantur” in the picture itself. Commons gives the date 1883 and links the Internet Archive scan it was taken from. The blue highlight was added by the Internet Archive's search tool; it is not in the book.

checked.note: Claude looked at the picture and read its Commons description page.

images.shows: The first page of a manuscript of Regino of Prüm's chronicle kept in the Stadtbibliothek Schaffhausen, Switzerland (shelfmark Min. 109). Verses fill the top; lower down a title reads “Chronicum Reginonis Abbatis Prumiensis”.
images.shows_basis: The library and shelfmark come from the Commons description, which links the e-codices page for Schaffhausen Min. 109. Claude read the title in the picture. When this copy was written has not been checked, so no date is given here.

checked.note: Claude looked at the picture and read its Commons description page.

images.file: File:Paris, BnF Ms Grec 2009 fol 93r-93v De Administrando Imperio - Chapter XXXII Of the Serbs.jpg
images.shows: Two pages (folios 93r–93v) of the Greek manuscript of De Administrando Imperio in the Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris (Ms. grec 2009). These pages are the start of chapter 32, on the Serbs, not chapter 38 on the Hungarians.
images.shows_basis: Library, shelfmark, folios and chapter come from the Commons description, which links the record in the Biblissima portal. Claude read the heading “Περὶ τῶν Σερβλων” (“On the Serbs”) in the picture. Commons dates the manuscript to the 12th century; that date has not been checked here.

checked.note: Claude looked at the picture and read its Commons description page.

images.file: File:Hincmarus Remensis, Adversus Hincmarum Laudunensem. - btv1b10550877n (025 of 553).jpg
images.shows: A page in verse from a manuscript of Hincmar's treatise against his nephew, Hincmar of Laon (Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Latin 2865). The library's catalogue calls the script “French, 9th century, school of Reims”, so the copy may have been made in Hincmar's own lifetime and city.
images.shows_basis: Shelfmark and the catalogue's description of the script are copied on Commons from the BnF catalogue (archivesetmanuscrits.bnf.fr, ark:/12148/cc60667q). The catalogue lists a verse preface on folios 1–5v; Claude saw that this page is in verse but did not check its folio number. “May have been made in his lifetime” is Claude's inference from the catalogue's date, not the catalogue's claim.

checked.note: Claude looked at the picture and read its Commons description page.

images.shows: Cemetery no. I at Karos as it looked in 2014, laid out as an open-air park. The carved wooden posts with labels are modern markers, not finds.
images.shows_basis: The Commons description says this is “cemetery Nr. I in Karos” in the Karos visitor centre (Karos Honfoglalás Kori Látogató Központ). That the posts are modern markers is Claude's reading of the photo and of the Commons category “Honfoglaláskori Régészeti Park, Karos” (archaeological park).

checked.note: Claude looked at the picture and read its Commons description page.

images.file: File:Temető rekonstrukció a karosi látogatóközpont udvarán (2015).JPG
images.shows: A modern reconstruction of a cemetery in the courtyard of the Karos visitor centre, photographed in 2015: wooden grave posts, wattle fences and an animal skull on a frame. It shows how the park's makers imagine a 10th-century cemetery, not what was found.
images.shows_basis: The Commons description (in Hungarian) calls it “Temető rekonstrukció”, a cemetery reconstruction, in the courtyard of the Karos visitor centre. Which finds, if any, the reconstruction is based on has not been checked.

checked.note: Claude looked at the picture and read its Commons description page.

images.file: File:Avar belt from grave in Biatorbagy hungary 8th cent IMG 0297.JPG
images.shows: A decorated belt strap-end on display in a museum. The photographer labels it as part of an Avar belt from a grave at Biatorbágy, Hungary, 8th century.
images.shows_basis: “Avar belt from grave in Biatorbagy, Hungary, 8th century” is the photographer's own file name and category on Commons; the museum's label has not been checked. The photo's recorded position is in central Budapest, where the Hungarian National Museum stands, but Commons does not name the museum.

checked.note: Claude looked at the picture and read its Commons description page.

images.file: File:Replica of the hun cauldron from Törtel (1).jpg
images.shows: A modern replica of the bronze cauldron found at Törtel, Hungary, one of the cauldrons usually linked with the Huns. It is a copy, photographed in a museum display in 2026.
images.shows_basis: The Commons description says “Replica of the hun cauldron from Törtel”. Where the original is kept, and why it is attributed to the Huns, have not been checked here; “usually linked with the Huns” is how Commons files it (category “Hun Empire”), not a checked claim.

checked.note: Claude looked at the picture and read its Commons description page.

images.file: File:Plaque with 3 Ibexes, 2nd-1st century BCE, Xiongnu.jpg
images.shows: An openwork metal plaque with three ibexes, which the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, dates to the 2nd–1st century BC and attributes to the Xiongnu.
images.shows_basis: Title, date and the Xiongnu attribution are the Metropolitan Museum's own, released by the museum under CC0 and copied to Commons with a link to the museum's record (metmuseum.org, object 49444). How the museum reached the attribution has not been checked.

checked.note: Claude looked at the picture and read its Commons description page.

commons.author: Metropolitan Museum of Art
commons.credit: Metropolitan Museum of Art Provided under CC0

images.shows: A coin with Arabic-script inscriptions from the Spillings Hoard, a Viking-age hoard found on Gotland, shown at Gotland Museum in Visby, Sweden. The photographer's description calls it a Khazar coin, the so-called “Moses coin”.
images.shows_basis: Hoard, museum and the name “Khazar coin, the so-called Moses coin” come from the photographer's Commons description. Who identified the coin as Khazar, and on what grounds, has not been checked, so treat the identification as the museum's or the photographer's, not ours.

checked.note: Claude looked at the picture and read its Commons description page.

images.shows: A page of the illustrated Madrid Skylitzes manuscript (folio 173r). The upper picture shows the Pechenegs killing the Rus of Sviatoslav of Kiev, an event of 972. The painter worked long after that, so the clothes and faces show the painter's ideas, not what Pechenegs looked like.
images.shows_basis: Folio and subject come from the Commons description, which links the Biblioteca Digital Hispánica (Biblioteca Nacional de España) copy and dates the manuscript to the 11th–13th centuries. The year 972 for Sviatoslav's death has not been checked against a source on this map.

checked.note: Claude looked at the picture and read its Commons description page.

images.file: File:Liutprand Antapodosis Beginning of text Munich Clm 6388 f 10r.jpg
images.shows: The first page of Liudprand's Antapodosis in a manuscript in the Bavarian State Library, Munich (Clm 6388, folio 10r). The heading reads “Incipit liber primus”, “Here begins the first book”. This page is the opening of the work, not the passage quoted on the card.
images.shows_basis: Shelfmark and folio come from the Commons description, which links the Munich library's digital copy. Claude read the heading in the picture. Commons dates the manuscript to the late 10th century, which has not been checked here.

checked.note: Claude looked at the picture and read its Commons description page.

images.file: File:Witichindi Saxonis Rerum ab Heinrico et Ottone I imp. gestarum libri 3, Basilea 1532.png
images.shows: The title page of the first printed edition of Widukind's Deeds of the Saxons, published in Basel in 1532 (“Witichindi Saxonis rerum ab Henrico et Ottone I impp. gestarum libri III”). The card quotes a modern English translation, not this edition.
images.shows_basis: Claude read the title and the imprint “Basileae apud Io. Hervagium … M.D.XXXII” in the picture. Commons calls it the editio princeps, the first printed edition, which has not been checked against a catalogue.

checked.note: Claude looked at the picture and read its Commons description page.

images.shows: The battle on the Lech in 955 as painted in a manuscript of the Saxon World Chronicle, about 300 years after the battle. Riders labelled “Ungari” (Hungarians) face Otto's army. The painter's armour and heraldry are of his own time, so this shows how the battle was imagined, not how it looked.
images.shows_basis: The Commons description gives the manuscript as Gotha, Forschungs- und Landesbibliothek, Ms. Memb. I 90, fol. 87v, dated about 1270, and says the picture was scanned from a book by Matthias Springer. Claude read the label “Ungari” in the picture. The date has not been checked against the library.

checked.note: Claude looked at the picture and read its Commons description page.

commons.author: Unknown author
commons.credit: Scan aus Buch: Matthias Springer, 955 als Zeitenwende - Otto I. und die Lechfeldschlacht, in: Matthias Puhle (Hrsg.): Otto der Große. Magdeburg und Europa, S.199-208, hier: S. 201.

images.file: File:Plaque with Christ Receiving Magdeburg Cathedral from Emperor Otto I MET DT143.jpg
images.shows: An ivory plaque in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, which the museum titles “Christ Receiving Magdeburg Cathedral from Emperor Otto I” and dates to about 962–968, in Otto's own lifetime. It is a religious image made for a church, not a portrait: the small kneeling figure offering the church is the museum's identification of Otto.
images.shows_basis: Title, date and the CC0 release come from the Metropolitan Museum, via the Commons file it donated (object 41.100.157). That the plaque is not a likeness is the usual reading of such donor images; it is Claude's caution, not the museum's words.

checked.note: Claude looked at the picture and read its Commons description page.

commons.author: Not stated on Commons

images.shows: The baptism of the Bulgar khan Boris, painted in the Madrid Skylitzes manuscript (folio 68v, detail), long after the event. The Annals of St-Bertin report the Bulgar ruler's baptism under 866.
images.shows_basis: Folio and subject come from the Commons description, which dates the manuscript to the 11th–13th centuries. That this is the same baptism as in the Frankish annals rests on both naming the Bulgar ruler's baptism in the 860s; the Byzantine chronicle itself has not been read for this map.

checked.note: Claude looked at the picture and read its Commons description page.

images.shows: A page of the Illuminated Chronicle (Chronicon Pictum), made about 1360, nearly five centuries after Árpád. Its large picture shows the Hungarians arriving in Pannonia, with Árpád on a white horse and tasting water from the Danube. It shows a 14th-century story, not evidence of Árpád's life or looks.
images.shows_basis: The Commons description (in Hungarian) gives page 21, the date 1360, and lists the scenes, naming Árpád on the white horse and Árpád tasting the Danube's water. Claude checked that the picture matches that description. The date and the painter's name given on Commons (Márk Kálti) have not been checked.

checked.note: Claude looked at the picture and read its Commons description page.

images.file: File:Artefacts - Early Sarmatians, mid - second half of 1mill BC - Museum of Archeology and Ethnography, Ufa.jpg
images.shows: A museum case of finds labelled as Early Sarmatian, from the middle to second half of the 1st millennium BC: daggers, horse bits, bronze mirrors, neck rings, beads and a pottery flask, in the Museum of Archaeology and Ethnography in Ufa, Bashkortostan.
images.shows_basis: The Commons description copies the museum's label, which names the period and lists the objects, including finds from the Bishungarovo and Zagrebalovo burial mounds in Bashkortostan. Claude saw the daggers, bits, mirrors and neck rings in the photo. The label's dates have not been checked against an excavation report.

checked.note: Claude looked at the picture and read its Commons description page.
